questions.stem: Absolute poverty is best defined as:
options: lacking the income to meet basic needs such as food, shelter and clothing
having an income well below the typical income in one's own local community
owning less wealth than the average household in the country
receiving any form of government transfer payment
questions.explanation: Absolute poverty is measured against a fixed standard of basic needs. Being well below the typical income in one's community is relative poverty.

questions.stem: Relative poverty refers to:
options: earning less than the highest-income households in the country
having no wealth at all, whatever a person's level of income
being unable to afford the living standard most people in the community enjoy
lacking enough food and shelter to survive, regardless of where a person lives
questions.explanation: Relative poverty is judged against the living standards of the community, so it changes as typical incomes rise. In Australia it is commonly measured as income below 50 per cent of median equivalised household income.

questions.stem: The difference between income and wealth is that:
options: income is a flow received over a period, while wealth is a stock of assets at a point in time
income is a stock of assets held at a point in time, while wealth is a flow over a given period
income includes only wages, while wealth includes all other earnings
income is taxed in Australia, while wealth is never counted by statisticians
questions.explanation: Income, such as wages, rent, interest and profit, is received over time. Wealth is the value of assets, such as housing, shares and superannuation, less debts, at a moment.

questions.stem: Transfer payments are:
options: payments by businesses to workers in return for their labour services
payments by households to the government in the form of income tax
payments by the government to firms for goods and services it buys
government payments to individuals with nothing provided in return
questions.explanation: Age pensions, unemployment benefits and family payments are transfers that redistribute income. Wages and government purchases are payments for goods, services or labour.

questions.stem: A welfare state is one in which:
options: all citizens receive exactly the same income regardless of their work
the government provides a safety net of payments and services
the government owns all businesses and sets every price in the economy
households must rely entirely on private charity during hardship
questions.explanation: A welfare state uses taxes to fund payments and services, such as pensions, health care and education, to reduce hardship. It does not require state ownership of all firms or equal incomes.

questions.stem: An egalitarian society is one that:
options: distributes income according to each person's inherited wealth
places a high value on equality of opportunity and a fair distribution of income
requires every household to receive exactly the same income each year
allows incomes to be set entirely by market forces, with no role at all for government
questions.explanation: Egalitarianism values fairness and reducing large gaps in income and opportunity. It need not mean identical incomes, which would weaken incentives.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a transfer payment in Australia?
options: JobSeeker Payment received by an unemployed person
Wages paid to a teacher at a state school
Government spending on a new hospital building
Interest paid to a household on its savings
questions.explanation: JobSeeker Payment is income support paid by the government with no good or service given in return. Wages and construction spending pay for labour or output, and interest is income from capital.

questions.stem: On a Lorenz curve diagram, the line of perfect equality shows that:
options: each percentage of households receives the same percentage of total income
the richest 20% of households receive all of the total income
income is distributed according to each household's productivity and effort
the poorest households receive no income at all
questions.explanation: Along the 45-degree line, the bottom 20% receive 20% of income, the bottom 50% receive 50%, and so on. The further the Lorenz curve sags below it, the greater the inequality.

questions.stem: The Gini coefficient is calculated from the Lorenz curve diagram as:
options: the slope of the Lorenz curve at the point where the poorest 50% of households are reached
the share of income received by the top 20% of households, divided by the bottom 20%
the total income of all households divided by the number of households in the country
the area between the equality line and Lorenz curve, over the area under the equality line
questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient compares the gap between equality and the actual distribution with the whole area under the equality line. It ranges from 0, perfect equality, to 1, where one household has all the income.

questions.stem: Australia's Gini coefficient for wealth is considerably higher than its Gini coefficient for income. This shows that:
options: income is distributed more unequally than wealth
households hold more income than wealth on average
wealth inequality is falling faster than income inequality
wealth is distributed more unequally than income
questions.explanation: A higher Gini coefficient means a more unequal distribution. Wealth accumulates over a lifetime and across generations through assets such as housing and shares, so it is more concentrated than income.

questions.stem: Why is median household income often preferred to mean household income as a measure of a typical household's income?
options: The median includes all incomes, while the mean leaves out the highest ones
The mean is always lower than the median because of low-income households
The median is calculated after tax, while the mean is calculated before tax
A few very high incomes raise the mean but have little effect on the median
questions.explanation: Income distributions are skewed, with a long tail of high earners that pulls the mean upwards. The median is the middle income, so it better represents a typical household.

questions.stem: In a small town, the incomes of five households are $30,000, $40,000, $50,000, $60,000 and $320,000. Which statement is correct?
options: The median is $100,000 and the mean is $50,000
The median and the mean are both $50,000
The median is $60,000 and the mean is $100,000
The median is $50,000 and the mean is $100,000
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value, $50,000. The mean is $500,000 / 5 = $100,000, pulled up by the one very high income.

questions.stem: Equivalence scales are used when comparing household incomes because:
options: larger households need more income to reach the same living standard
households with more members always have higher living standards than smaller ones
income must be converted into wealth before households can be compared
they remove the effect of taxation from household income data
questions.explanation: A family of four needs more income than a single person, but not four times as much, because some costs are shared. Equivalence scales adjust income for household size and composition.

questions.stem: Using the modified OECD equivalence scale (1 for the first adult, 0.5 for each other person aged 15 or over, 0.3 for each child under 15), a couple with two young children has a disposable income of $105,000. Its equivalised income is:
questions.explanation: The scale gives 1 + 0.5 + 0.3 + 0.3 = 2.1, and $105,000 / 2.1 = $50,000. Dividing by four people instead gives $26,250, which ignores shared costs.

questions.stem: The Henderson poverty line, first set by a national inquiry into poverty in the 1970s, is:
options: the income level at which households begin to pay income tax
a measure of the share of total national wealth held by the richest 10% of households
an income benchmark for household types, below which households are counted as poor
the minimum wage that employers must pay adult workers in Australia
questions.explanation: The Henderson line set income benchmarks based on a reference family and has been updated over time in line with community incomes. It is distinct from the minimum wage or the tax-free threshold.

questions.stem: A relative poverty line is set at 50 per cent of median equivalised household income. If all incomes rise by 10 per cent, the number of households in relative poverty will:
options: rise, as the poverty line rises faster than household incomes
fall to zero, as no household remains below the old fixed poverty line at all
stay the same, as the poverty line rises by the same proportion as incomes
fall, as every household now has a higher income than before
questions.explanation: A relative line moves with the median, so an equal proportional rise in every income leaves each household in the same position relative to the line. Absolute poverty would fall, as real incomes have risen.

questions.stem: Household income data are often reported as disposable income. Disposable income is:
options: income left over after all spending on necessities such as food
gross income, including transfers, less income tax and the Medicare levy
gross income before any income tax or transfer payments are counted
the total value of a household's assets less its debts
questions.explanation: Disposable income is what a household has available to spend or save after paying income tax. The value of assets less debts is wealth, a stock rather than a flow.

questions.stem: In Country A the poorest 40% of households receive 25% of total income; in Country B they receive 15%. Which statement is correct?
options: Country B's poorest households receive more than the line of equality would give them
Country B's Lorenz curve lies further below the line of equality at this point
Country A's Lorenz curve lies further below the line of equality at this point
Country A has more income inequality, as its poorest households earn a larger share
questions.explanation: With perfect equality the poorest 40% would receive 40% of income. Country B's share is further from that, so its Lorenz curve sags more at this point, suggesting greater inequality.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why workers with university degrees tend to earn more than those with no post-school qualifications?
options: Higher educational attainment raises skills and productivity
University graduates are required by law to be paid higher wages
Workers without degrees choose to work fewer hours each week
Graduates pay lower rates of income tax than other workers
questions.explanation: Education and training build skills that are scarce and valued, so graduates can command higher wages. Educational attainment is a major source of income differences in Australia.

questions.stem: Employment status is a major cause of income inequality because:
options: people without work rely on transfer payments well below typical wage incomes
unemployed people receive higher incomes than people working in part-time jobs
full-time workers pay no tax, so their disposable income is higher
employment has no link to the income a household receives
questions.explanation: Wages are the main source of income for most households, so unemployment or underemployment sharply lowers income. Transfer payments provide a safety net but are typically far below average earnings.

questions.stem: Why does the uneven distribution of the factors of production lead to inequality of both income and wealth?
options: Land and capital earn no income, so their ownership does not affect inequality
Workers receive all national income, so owning assets makes no difference to inequality
Owners of land and capital earn rent, interest and profit, which can build more wealth
Every household owns an equal share of capital, so only wages differ between households
questions.explanation: Households that own property and shares earn income from those assets, and can save and invest it to accumulate further. Those who own only their labour depend on wages, so gaps can widen over time.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how age contributes to wealth inequality?
options: Younger households receive more inheritance on average than older households do
Retirees earn the highest wage incomes in the economy
Wealth is distributed equally across all age groups in Australia
Older households have had longer to pay off homes and build superannuation
questions.explanation: Wealth builds up over a working life through home ownership, superannuation and savings, so it tends to peak near retirement. Younger households typically have fewer assets and more debt.

questions.stem: Women in Australia have, on average, lower lifetime incomes and superannuation balances than men. A contributing factor is that:
options: women pay higher rates of income tax than men on the same income
women are not permitted to contribute to superannuation funds
women are more likely to take career breaks or work part-time to care for others
employers are required by law to pay women less than men for doing the same work
questions.explanation: Time out of paid work and part-time hours reduce earnings and super contributions, and female-dominated industries tend to pay less. Equal pay for equal work is required by law.

questions.stem: Family structure can contribute to inequality because:
options: single-parent households have only one potential earner but similar costs
single-parent households always receive more income than couple households
couples with children have lower costs than single people living alone
family structure has no effect on household income or living costs
questions.explanation: A household with one adult has less earning capacity, and caring duties may limit work hours, so single-parent families face higher rates of poverty. Transfer payments partly offset this.

questions.stem: Recently arrived migrants with overseas qualifications are sometimes employed in jobs below their skill level. This contributes to inequality mainly because:
options: qualifications not recognised locally reduce the wages migrants can earn
migrants are not permitted to work in Australia for their first five years
migrants pay higher income tax rates than other workers on the same income
migrants receive higher transfer payments than other low-income households
questions.explanation: When overseas skills or qualifications are not recognised, or language and networks are barriers, workers may earn less than their abilities would justify. Skills recognition programs aim to address this.

questions.stem: People living with disability are more likely to have low incomes. A key reason is that:
options: people with disability are not eligible for any government support
people with disability pay higher tax rates than other workers
employers are required to pay people with disability lower wages
barriers to employment can limit their access to paid work
questions.explanation: Lower rates of employment and additional living costs leave many people with disability on low incomes. Supports such as the Disability Support Pension and the NDIS aim to reduce disadvantage.

questions.stem: Which is a social cost of high and persistent income inequality?
options: Higher incentives for everyone to work and take risks
Faster growth in the incomes of the lowest-income households than in others
Lower spending by government on welfare and health care
Poorer health and education outcomes that limit people's opportunities
questions.explanation: Large gaps can lead to worse health, lower educational attainment and reduced social cohesion, which can pass disadvantage between generations. These are costs to society, not only to individuals.

questions.stem: Some inequality is said to have economic benefits. The main argument is that:
options: inequality means resources go to those with the lowest skills
differences in rewards create incentives to work, study, invest and innovate
inequality guarantees that every household's income rises in each and every year
high inequality always reduces the need for government spending
questions.explanation: If higher effort, skill and risk-taking earn higher rewards, people have reasons to build skills and start businesses. Very high inequality, though, can limit opportunity and waste talent.

questions.stem: A progressive income tax helps reduce income inequality because:
options: lower-income earners pay a larger proportion of their income in income tax
it is collected only from businesses and not from individuals
higher-income earners pay a larger proportion of their income in tax
all taxpayers pay the same proportion of their income in tax
questions.explanation: Rising marginal rates mean average tax rates increase with income, narrowing the gap in disposable incomes. A tax taking the same proportion from everyone is proportional, not progressive.

questions.stem: The Age Pension is means-tested, so payments are reduced for people with higher income or assets. This design mainly aims to:
options: encourage retirees to sell their homes and spend their savings
raise revenue for the government from wealthy retirees
direct support to those most in need while limiting the cost to taxpayers
pay all retirees exactly the same amount regardless of their personal circumstances
questions.explanation: Means testing targets transfers to people with limited resources, so a given budget does more to reduce poverty. A drawback is that the payment reduces as private income rises, which can weaken incentives to work or save.

questions.stem: Government subsidisation of merit goods such as Medicare and public schools reduces inequality mainly because:
options: it replaces all income tax with charges for using services
all households can access essential services regardless of their income
only high-income households are allowed to use these services
it raises the prices that low-income households pay for health care
questions.explanation: Providing health care and education free or at low cost gives low-income households services they might otherwise go without. This raises their living standards and their future earning capacity.

questions.stem: Which is a possible private cost of redistributing income through higher taxes and transfers?
options: Low-income households gain more access to health care and education
Social cohesion improves as income gaps narrow
Consumer spending rises as income moves to households that spend more of it
High effective tax rates may reduce some people's incentive to work extra hours
questions.explanation: When extra earnings are heavily taxed or cause transfer payments to be withdrawn, the gain from working more is small. The other options describe benefits of redistribution.

questions.stem: Moving income from high-income to low-income households may raise total consumer spending because:
options: redistribution raises the incomes of every household at the same time
low-income households spend a larger share of each extra dollar they receive
high-income households spend all of their income and save nothing
low-income households save a larger share of each extra dollar they receive
questions.explanation: Lower-income households have a higher marginal propensity to consume, so a dollar transferred to them is more likely to be spent. This is one of the economic arguments for redistribution.

questions.stem: Commonwealth Rent Assistance is paid to eligible low-income renters, but critics argue part of its benefit may flow to landlords. This illustrates that:
options: transfer payments always raise the incomes of their recipients by the full amount
rent assistance is a form of progressive taxation paid by landlords
redistribution has no effect on the prices of goods and services
an intervention can have unintended consequences that reduce its effectiveness
questions.explanation: If extra assistance raises renters' ability to pay where housing supply is limited, rents may rise, so landlords capture some of the payment. Evaluating policy means considering such effects.

questions.stem: A government wants to reduce inequality of opportunity over the long term rather than only income gaps today. Which strategy best fits this aim?
options: Cutting the top marginal income tax rate to reward high earners
Reducing the rate of the GST on luxury goods
Increasing funding for early childhood education in disadvantaged areas
Giving a one-off cash payment to all households in the current financial year
questions.explanation: Early education builds skills that raise future earning capacity, tackling a root cause of inequality. A one-off payment eases hardship now but does not change long-term opportunities.
